title: Nurses' experiences regarding role boundaries in collaborative AI-Assisted nursing: A meta-synthesis.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly integrating into the nursing field, evolving from simple assistive tools to complex applications that transform nursing practice models, thereby profoundly impacting the professional jurisdiction of nurses. Given the lack of systematic theoretical integration in existing research, this study employs Abbott's Jurisdictional Framework and uses meta-synthesis to reveal how nurses construct and maintain their professional jurisdiction in AI-assisted nursing, as well as the institutional conditions that facilitate or constrain this process. A systematic search of six major databases, including PubMed and Embase, identified 12 high-quality qualitative studies from the Netherlands, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan, China, Bangladesh, Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Data analysis followed Thomas and Harden's three-phase thematic synthesis: Phases 1 and 2 involved inductive coding to generate 22 descriptive themes; Phase 3 incorporated Abbott's Jurisdictional Framework to synthesize and elevate these into 7 analytical themes. Nurses do not passively accept technology in human-machine collaboration but actively engage in "boundary work." They ensure their leading role in clinical reasoning by exercising "final verification authority" and "decision deviation authority," while upholding their right to make personalized treatment adjustments. Facing technological disruption, nurses establish a professional core barrier distinct from machines by emphasizing the irreplaceability of "humanistic care." However, this adaptation process faces significant obstacles in legal liability determination, skills training, and social trust building, hindering effective nurse-AI collaboration. The jurisdictional integration between AI and nursing remains in a transitional state of "not yet achieved." At cognitive and discursive levels, nurses are active boundary-makers; at institutional and organizational levels, they are responders to structural constraints. Achieving a sustainable human-machine collaboration ecosystem requires systematic support through legal liability clarification, algorithm literacy education, and organizational resource optimization.
